correctness.rationale: Prime-power totients of the distinct prime factors must divide 8q. For q≥7 the only support is 2,3,5 and prime r_i=2^i q+1; the odd exponents are at most one. Exact q-adic valuation forces one r_i per solution, not one prime candidate per q. The remaining 2-adic budget is 3−i; φ(2^u) contributes zero valuation for both u=0 and u=1. This gives multipliers {5,8,10,12}, {3,4,6}, {1,2}; substituting proves sufficiency. Modulo 3 exactly the claimed families are excluded, and surviving families are disjoint by large prime support. The exceptional support/exponent check and an independently written bounded totient sieve agree with both exceptional lists. The sieve through 96000 compared complete sets for the 302 odd primes ≤2000, with 503 solutions. For q≥7, n/φ(n)≤2·(3/2)·(5/4)·(r_i/(r_i−1))<6; for q=3,5 multiplying the corresponding factors over the full respective allowed supports gives <6 as well. The sizes 0,2,3,4,6,9,10 are realized at q=19,17,7,23,11,5,3, respectively. The valuation proof, not the sieve, proves the unrestricted claim.
residual_risks: The numerical reproduction is finite; there is no machine-checked general proof in the package.

value.rationale: As mathematics the result is a natural complete first slice of an explicitly posed inverse-totient family, not a recomputation of the small tables. It characterizes empty fibers and all integers in nonempty ones via a small exact primality test. This intrinsic value does not give a second equivalent record distinct value over the indexed classification, and does not overcome the originality failure.
residual_risks: The result classifies the 8q slice only; it does not determine frequencies of the prime conditions or settle the wider family.
